## Learning Objectives

- Explain the assumptions of Poisson regression.
- Define, use, and interpret the term "offset".


## Lesson

Poisson regression has the following assumptions:

1. $Y_i|X_{i1},\dotsc,X_{ip}\sim\text{Poisson}(\lambda_i t_i)$.
2. $\log\lambda_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 X_{i1} + \cdots + \beta_p X_{ip}$.
3. The observations are iid.

This is the first time we're not modeling a mean.
Here, we're modeling $\lambda_i$, which is a rate.
We can model the mean if we include something called an "offset":
$$
\begin{align*}
\log\lambda_i &= \beta_0 + \beta_1 X_{i1} + \cdots + \beta_p X_{ip} \\
\log\lambda_i + \log t_i &= \beta_0 + \beta_1 X_{i1} + \cdots + \beta_p X_{ip} + \log t_i \\
\log \left(\lambda_i t_i\right) &= \beta_0 + \beta_1 X_{i1} + \cdots + \beta_p X_{ip} + \log t_i \\
\log \mu_i &= \beta_0 + \beta_1 X_{i1} + \cdots + \beta_p X_{ip} + \underbrace{\log t_i}_{\text{offset}} \text{.} \\
\end{align*}
$$

The offset is the additional term, $\log t_i$,
that is added to the linear model so that we can model the mean
instead of the rate.



## Problems

### Problem 1

If $t_i = 1$,
what is $\log \mu_i$?

::: {.callout-tip title="Solution" collapse="true"}

If $t_i = 1$ then $\log t_i = \log 1 = 0$, so
$$
\log \mu_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 X_{i1} + \cdots + \beta_p X_{ip} \text{.}
$$
Another way of saying this is that if $t_i = 1$ then $\mu_i = \lambda_i$.

:::

### Problem 2

Which of the four assumptions of linear regression are automatically violated
when the outcome is a count?

::: {.callout-tip title="Solution" collapse="true"}

The assumption that the random errors are normally distributed,
conditional on the explanatory variables,
is automatically violated.
Suppose $E(Y_i|X_{i1},\dotsc,X_{ip})$ is 3.5.
The only possible random errors are $\{-3.5,-2.5,-1.5,-0.5,0.5,1.5,2.5,3.5,\dotsc\}$
because the outcome needs to be in $\{0,1,2,3,4,5,6,7,\dotsc\}$.
A normally distributed random variable can be any real number.
So, the errors can't be normally distributed.

The assumption of constant variance is not automatically violated,
but it is often violated.
Suppose the outcome is Poisson-distributed.
Recall that the mean of the Poisson distribution is equal to its variance.
So, the variance will change as the mean changes.

:::
